motivation: In 2007 Lorimer, McLaughlin and Bailes found a single, extremely bright, millisecond radio burst in archival Parkes pulsar-survey data. Its dispersion measure placed it far outside the Milky Way. This was the first fast radio burst. It opened a new class of astrophysical phenomenon, built on McLaughlin's earlier discovery of rotating radio transients and on Bailes's single-pulse search methods. Since then, thousands of FRBs have been detected, including repeaters, and one has been linked to a Galactic magnetar. They are now localized to host galaxies. FRBs have become precise probes of the ionized intergalactic medium, measuring the cosmic baryon budget that was missing from galaxies, and constraining intergalactic magnetic fields. They also probe the most extreme magnetized neutron stars. The discovery came from careful pulsar instrumentation and search algorithms. It created an entire field of transient physics and an important new cosmological tool.
